nodes.question: What types of teams were involved in applying and testing the approach?
nodes.answer: Interdisciplinary project teams from the CSIRO S Valuing Sustainability Future Science Platform were involved in applying and testing the approach.
nodes.paragraph: At a practical level, the approach can be used to self-assess and catalyse readiness for engagement within these teams. We examine if the approach has the accessibility, practical utility, and theoretical depth to enable re exivity and learning to prepare teams for co-production praxis. We applied and tested the approach with interdisciplinary project teams to develop an early iteration of their engagement plans within their projects. Capability developed prior to engagement is anticipated to manifest initially as opportunities for different forms of learning. We use a modi ed analytical framework based on domains of learning (after Brymer et al. 2018 , Baird et al. 2014 ) to analyse how the approach facilitated learning and re exivity. These teams were drawn from within CSIRO S Valuing Sustainability Future Science Platform, an investment to build capacity to address sustainability challenges using transdisciplinary research. Insights from this analysis are discussed, including how the approach facilitates re exivity via multiple learning domains and rapidly via diagnostic questions that go to the heart of rich threads of learning across project contexts and teams. ORIGINAL PAPER HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES COMMUNICATIONS From a theoretical context to a diagnostic framework for co-production In this section we draw on literature reviewed from collaboration and co-production literature in sustainability, science and tech-nology studies, environmental management, learning and trans- disciplinary sciences and expert core team perspectives to formulate a methodologically robust but intuitively accessible framework for diagnosing co-production (examined empirically in section 3).

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: Why are place-based solutions focusing on households considered more viable?
nodes.answer: Place-based solutions focusing on households are considered more viable because they are relevant and practical for the local community, making them easier to adopt than externally generated solutions.
nodes.paragraph: Target 11.6: By 2030, reduce the adverse per capita environmental impact of cities, including by paying special attention to air quality and municipal and other waste management. 2 Proper waste management contributes to SDG 12 substantially reduce waste generation, ensuring that there is sustainable consump- tion and production patterns. Target 12.5: By 2030, substantially reduce waste generation through prevention, reduction, recycling and reuse. 59 Socio-Ecological Practice Research (2025) 7:57 76 for agriculture, and threaten the livelihoods of communities that depend on natural resources. Focusing on households generates place-based solutions that are relevant and practi- cal for the local community, making them easier to adopt than externally generated solutions. This approach also con- tributes to strategies for achieving SDGs 11 and 12. We are mindful that industries contribute seventy times more waste than households (Rogers 2005 , p. 4). However, we argue that individuals in households who consume industry goods, are the drivers of high waste generation in industries. shows how households and industries create a positive feed- back loop. The demand for industry goods is influenced by self- serving model of capitalist industries that make products with built-in obsolescence and the promotion of frenetic consumer culture (Rogers 2006, p. 219 of 558).
